source.title: Descriptive Collision in Sparse Autoencoder Auto-Interpretability: When One Explanation Describes Many Features

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies collisions among natural-language annotations of SAE features. It does not test superposition, feature geometry, capacity pressure, feature recovery, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper reports empirical results about reuse and specificity of human-written SAE annotations, not about the representation or geometry of the features themselves. Its discussion of other critiques and its proposed scoring procedures are not results testing the claim.
record.test_reason: The study reanalyzes human-written annotation strings for 722 SAE features and counts how often labels are reused. This is a property of the label space, not of the features. The authors say so directly: collision is "a property of the label space, not of the feature dictionary." No result bears on toy-model geometry (V1), capacity (V2/V3), distributed features or SAE recovery in LLMs (V4), whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical (V5), or feature dimensionality (V6). Its mention of non-canonical SAE features (Leask et al.; Paulo & Belrose) is cited work, not its own result.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors add that collision is distinct from, and additive to, polysemanticity and other auto-interp failure modes. They also expect machine-generated labels to collide at least as much as human ones, but they do not test this.
record.recipe_differences: The study reanalyzes human annotation data and proposes label-scoring methods; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported annotation resolution differs between the Gemma 2 2B corpus (61.8% of max) and the Pythia 70M corpus (80.9% of max).

fits_no_version.finding: In the Marks et al. corpus of 722 human-annotated SAE features: 82.1% share an annotation string with another feature, and only 235 unique strings appear. The string 'plural nouns' labels 101 features across 18 layer/component sites. Annotations resolve 6.65 of 9.50 bits of feature identity (70%). Detection-style scoring is shown, by a trivial proposition, to be invariant to collision.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Short natural-language labels for SAE features are highly non-identifying: many distinct features share one label, so high explanation scores do not certify which feature is meant.

record.problems: The empirical analysis is limited to one corpus of 722 human-annotated features. The paper does not measure collision rates for machine-generated labels; its expectation that these would be higher is not empirically tested. The proposed discrimination score is not evaluated on new labels or judge outputs.
record.rows_left_out: No reported findings about annotation-string distribution were omitted. Theoretical propositions, proposed scoring methods, and results cited from other work were not entered as rows because they do not report a test of the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: no capacity or importance analysis.
All: no analysis of why neurons are polysemantic.
All: no measurement of feature distribution or SAE recovery; SAE features are taken as given.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features. Only label distinctiveness is measured. The cross-layer reuse of 'plural nouns' is not a test of feature canonicity.

record.verdict_notes: Internal inconsistencies in the source. Subset counts sum to 747, but 722 are reported after removing a single duplicate. Figure 2 shows top-20 coverage of 49.7% in the plot but 50.1% in the caption. Limitation 4 concedes that some same-label features may be genuinely redundant model representations, which would make collision informative about the model. This is untested and does not bear on V5 as stated.

versions.untested_parts: Feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry in toy networks.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or sparse features can be recovered by a dictionary.
Whether SAE features themselves are complete, stable, canonical units; the paper measures annotation distinctiveness, not feature completeness or stability.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Marks et al. annotated SAE feature corpus
rows.size_stated: 722 features; 470 annotated features from Gemma 2 2B SAEs and 277 from Pythia 70M SAEs before deduplication
rows.operation_detail: Counted distinct annotation strings across the deduplicated corpus
rows.note: Describes annotation reuse, not feature representation geometry.
rows.check: Value 235 unique strings is correct. The size field passes on the paper's own inconsistency: 470 + 277 = 747, yet the paper says one duplicate was removed to reach 722. The state 'observed' has no version-relative meaning; the row describes the annotation corpus, not superposition.
